# Email config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/email/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.EmailBlock` — the deployment's one email service (ADR-169): the address it sends as and how it submits mail. A singleton kind: at most one `email` block across the vault, and a second file is refused naming both.

**Declared in the system vault alone.** The block names the deployment's mail credential and the address tera sends as, so an `.tera/email/` directory in any other vault — a repository vault or a plugin vault — is refused under every `deployment_profile` (degraded at mount, `email_outside_system_vault` at `tera config plan` and `tera config validate`), and a role granting `vaults/contribute/email` is refused at load.

**Presence is enablement.** No block, no service: nothing is constructed, no connection is opened and nothing is created on disk. There is no bootstrap-HCL spelling to fall back to, so withdrawing the last file here composes to no service rather than to a boot-time value.

**The credential is a reference.** `smtp.password` names where the password is read from and is resolved for each message, so a rotation behind an unchanged reference needs no restart; a bare literal is refused outside the dev posture, by the same rule the Telegram bot token takes. The mailbox password in `imap {}` is a reference by the same rule, resolved at every connection. TLS is never an attribute: implicit TLS on port 465 (SMTP) and 993 (IMAP), STARTTLS required on any other, plaintext never.

The sending half decodes, with `enrollment_content_class` — the content class a code sign-in's enrolment stamps on the person's email correspondence window (absent: undeclared, served terse) — and the receiving half's `receive "<address>" { imap {} correspondence {} }`: one mailbox read for one address, whose replies answer the questions correspondence emailed. At most one `receive` names `correspondence {}`, and declaring it is what puts Reply-To and the `-- Reply above this line --` delimiter on correspondence mail. A `receive` naming `input_adapter {}` instead makes the address an input adapter of that name: a trigger declaring `input_adapter "<address>" {}` is handed each message read from the mailbox. The `api {}` sender and the `webhook {}` source do not decode yet: each lands with the runtime that honours it. The per-consumer send rates are not here: every bound on what a subsystem may cost is declared in `admission`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `config/email` |
| Regime | persisted |
| Identity regime | `singleton` — the kind itself is the identity; neither the stem nor a label carries meaning (ADR-087 D3) |
| Current version | `v1` |
| Supported versions | `v1` |
| HCL block | `email` |

## Example

A minimal `email`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/email/example-email.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

email {
  from = "tera@example.com"

  smtp {
    host     = "smtp.example.com"
    port     = 587
    username = "tera@example.com"
    password = "env://EXAMPLE_CREDENTIAL"
  }
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `from` | string | yes | — | — | — | The address every message the email service sends is From — one address, written bare (tera@example.com), with no display name and no angle brackets; the display name is display_name. It must be an address the smtp account may send as: a provider rewrites or refuses a From the authenticated account does not own, so on the Gmail golden path it is the account's own address or a send-as alias configured on it. |
| `display_name` | string | no | — | — | — | The name a mail client shows beside the from address ("Example tera"). Optional; unset sends the bare address. Plain text on one line: it is placed in the From header, so a line break is refused at load rather than allowed to start a second header. |
| `smtp` | block | no | — | — | — | How the service sends: SMTP submission to the provider's server, authenticated with a username and a password reference. Exactly one sending block is required, and smtp is the only one this version defines — an email block with none is refused at load, because both of the service's consumers (the sign-in door's mail and the correspondence carrier) depend on sending. |
| `enrollment_content_class` | string | no | — | — | — | The content class (terse or full) stamped on an email correspondence window when a code sign-in enrols the address it verified. Optional; absent stamps no class, which is undeclared and served terse on every deployment_profile — the fact of a message and none of its content. A deployment doing client work sets full once: a code-enrolled window belongs to a person who has just signed in, and what it is mailed is what that person can already see. Read at each enrolment, so an edit changes the windows enrolled next and none already enrolled; a window's class is changed afterwards by api/v1/correspondence/content-class. |
| `receive` | block (list) | no | — | — | — | One receiving address, the label: tera reads its mailbox and hands each message to the one consumer the block names. Repeatable, one block per address; two labels naming the same address — compared as the email service compares addresses, so case and an internationalized domain's spelling do not make two — are refused at load. Mail is routed by which mailbox it was read from, never by its To, Cc or Delivered-To headers, which a sender writes. At most one receive names correspondence {}. |

**Exactly one of** `smtp`.

## `smtp` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `host` | string | yes | — | — | — | The submission server's host name (smtp.gmail.com). A bare host — no scheme, no port; the port is its own attribute. The server's certificate is verified against this name. |
| `port` | integer | yes | — | — | — | The submission port. 465 is implicit TLS: the connection is TLS from its first byte. Any other port — 587 is the usual — requires STARTTLS, and a server that does not offer it is refused rather than spoken to in plaintext. There is no attribute to change either rule. |
| `username` | string | yes | — | — | — | The account the service authenticates to the submission server as — on the Gmail golden path, the full address of the mailbox (tera@example.com). Not a secret, and printed on the boot line. |
| `password` | string | yes | — | — | — | A CREDENTIAL REFERENCE to the submission password — keychain://name, env://VAR, vault://path or secret://name — and never the password itself. On the Gmail golden path it names a Google app password. Resolved for each message the service sends rather than once at boot, so rotating the material behind an unchanged reference takes effect on the next message with no restart. This block is authored in a vault file and a vault is a git tree, so a bare literal is refused on every deployment profile but dev, where it warns; literal://<value> is the escape hatch for an operator who means it, and warns on every profile. The resolved value is never logged, never returned in an error and never written to a record: the boot line and every operator surface print the reference, and withhold a literal. |

## `receive` block

Repeatable.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `address` | string | yes | — | — | block label | The receiving address, written bare (tera@example.com): the address people reply to, and the mailbox the source reads. On the Gmail golden path it is the from address, so a reply to a question comes back to the mailbox it was sent from. |
| `imap` | block | no | — | — | — | Where the address's mail is read from: an IMAP mailbox, polled read-only. Exactly one source is required, and imap is the only one this version defines. The mailbox stays the operator's: tera fetches without setting a flag, moving or deleting, and keeps its own cursor in the daemon's database, starting at the mail that arrives after the source is first configured. |
| `correspondence` | block | no | — | — | — | Who the address's mail is for: correspondence, which reads each message as a reply to a question tera emailed. Exactly one consumer is required: correspondence or input_adapter. Declaring it is what makes every correspondence email carry Reply-To this address and the -- Reply above this line -- delimiter; the text above the delimiter is the answer. Attribution grants nothing: only a sender whose provider reported dmarc=pass for the From domain is presented as that address, and correspondence then admits or refuses it as it admits any window — a refused sender is never answered. |
| `input_adapter` | block | no | — | — | — | Who the address's mail is for: the triggers bound to it. The address becomes an input adapter of that name, in the email service's canonical form (lower-case, an internationalized domain in A-labels), and a trigger declaring input_adapter "<address>" {} with that name is handed each message read from this mailbox as its payload: message_id (email:<received-record-id>), rfc_message_id, from, to, cc, subject, text, received_at, verdicts (spf, dkim, dmarc, dmarc_aligned), attributed, sender_principal (only when attributed) and attachments (metadata only, never their bytes). The event's headers, query, topic and payload_text are empty, so no header a sender writes is readable by a predicate, and the message reaches only the triggers bound to the address it was read from, whatever its To or Cc say. Attribution grants nothing: the Work Order runs with the trigger's worker and authority, and the sender's principal is a payload field. Each message is handed over at most once; a DSN, auto-submitted mail and a malformed or too-large message reach no trigger. |

**Exactly one of** `imap`.

**Exactly one of** `correspondence` | `input_adapter`.

## `receive.imap` block

Nested under `receive`.

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `host` | string | yes | — | — | — | The IMAP server's host name (imap.gmail.com). A bare host — no scheme, no port; the port is its own attribute. The server's certificate is verified against this name. |
| `port` | integer | yes | — | — | — | The IMAP port. 993 is implicit TLS: the connection is TLS from its first byte. Any other port requires STARTTLS, and a server that does not offer it is refused rather than spoken to in plaintext. There is no attribute to change either rule. |
| `username` | string | yes | — | — | — | The account the source logs in to the mailbox as — on the Gmail golden path, the mailbox's full address. Not a secret, and printed on the boot line. |
| `password` | string | yes | — | — | — | A CREDENTIAL REFERENCE to the mailbox password — keychain://name, env://VAR, vault://path or secret://name — and never the password itself. On the Gmail golden path it names a Google app password. Resolved at every connection rather than once at boot, so a rotation behind an unchanged reference takes effect at the next connection with no restart. A bare literal is refused on every deployment profile but dev, where it warns; literal://<value> warns on every profile. The resolved value is never logged, never returned in an error and never written to a record. |
| `authserv_id` | string | no | — | — | — | The authserv-id the receiving provider stamps on the Authentication-Results header it adds (mx.google.com for Gmail). A message's SPF, DKIM and DMARC verdicts are read from the topmost Authentication-Results header carrying this id and from no other, because a sender can write the header but not above the one the provider adds; tera evaluates none of them itself. Optional, and declare it only for a provider that always adds one: absent, no message has verdicts, so no sender is ever presented as its From address and correspondence refuses every reply as from an unenrolled sender. |
